events.text:
⚡🇪🇺🛢️ IEA: Diesel Markets to Stay Tight Well Into 2027
The International Energy Agency warned that global diesel supplies are likely to remain constrained well into 2027. The main causes are the Iran war's disruption of Middle East refining and exports and Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries. In its monthly Oil Market Report, the agency said combined net gasoil/diesel exports from the Middle East and Russia fell by 1.3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, to 820,000 b/d in September. Higher shipments from the US and China only partly offset the loss. European diesel refining margins hit a record of almost $95 a barrel in September. Wholesale diesel prices topped $200 a barrel. The IEA expects refinery output to recover and return to a seasonal surplus in early 2027, but says rebuilding depleted inventories is unlikely before the second half of 2027. G7 leaders pledged on 2 October to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks over four months. That pledge largely accelerates delivery of an IEA release agreed in March rather than adding new barrels. The IEA warned that oil markets "may experience more turmoil in the months ahead."

events.text:
🚀 135 strikes, 84 sites: Iran’s precision campaign reshapes the Gulf
A months-long Reuters investigation found that Iran and allied forces carried out at least 135 drone and missile strikes on 84 infrastructure sites across the Gulf after the US and Israel began bombing Iran on February 28. The attacks repeatedly hit critical equipment, including targets only a few meters wide or hidden inside buildings.
A former US Marine Corps strike coordinator who reviewed the evidence described the campaign as showing “precision, targeting expertise, and patience.” Reuters said the strikes helped Iran withstand pressure from the far more powerful US military and gave Tehran major leverage over regional energy flows and negotiations.
The targets were not random. Iran repeatedly struck Fujairah’s oil-routing systems, Qatar’s Ras Laffan LNG complex and Saudi pipeline infrastructure used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. At Fujairah, refined-fuel exports essentially stopped for a month after another Iranian strike in May.
The investigation also found Gulf governments repeatedly downplayed the damage, often blaming falling debris from successful interceptions. Reuters said experts reviewing the evidence considered it highly improbable that such precise damage to vital equipment was caused by debris alone.
The broader picture is stark: Washington launched a war against Iran expecting overwhelming military superiority. Months later, Reuters’ own evidence shows Tehran systematically exploiting the Gulf’s most vulnerable pressure points and forcing the region to reckon with the cost of that war.
